summary: This document introduces a hub and spoke multipoint (HSMP) Label Switched Path, which carries traffic from the root to the leaves along a point-to-multipoint LSP and also from leaves back to the root along the reverse path. It does this with extensions to LDP.

eli5.summary: Picture a bus route where the hub sends passengers out to every stop, and every stop can also send passengers back to the hub. This adds that to a network.

subtitle: A multipoint label switched path that fans out from a hub to every spoke, while spokes can only talk back to the hub.

tldr.problem: A point-to-multipoint LSP carries traffic only from the root to the leaves, and a multipoint-to-multipoint LSP lets every node reach every other node. Neither fits a hub and spoke design where leaves talk only to the root.
tldr.mechanism: A hub and spoke multipoint (HSMP) LSP pairs a downstream P2MP tree with an upstream path that follows the same tree in reverse and ends only at the root. LDP gets two new FEC types and a capability to signal it.
tldr.outcome: Leaves can send to the root and the root can send to all leaves, with no direct leaf-to-leaf traffic. RFC 7140 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7358.

today: RFC 7140 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7358. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Hub and Spoke Multipoint LSPs
sections.content:
A point-to-multipoint (P2MP) Label Switched Path (LSP), defined in RFC 6388, carries traffic from a root to several leaf nodes. A multipoint-to-multipoint (MP2MP) LSP carries traffic from every node to every other node. RFC 7140 adds a third shape, the hub and spoke multipoint (HSMP) LSP, which has one root node and one or more leaf nodes.

Traffic that enters at the root travels down the tree exactly as it would on a P2MP LSP. Traffic that enters at any leaf travels up toward the root only. The upstream path is like a unicast LSP to the root, except that it follows the reverse of the downstream tree instead of the path chosen by the routing protocol. Together, the upstream paths from all leaves form a multipoint-to-point LSP. Direct communication among leaf nodes is not allowed.
sections.eli5: The hub can shout to everyone at once. Anyone else can only whisper back to the hub, and the hub decides what everyone hears.

sections.title: How an HSMP LSP Is Built
sections.content:
An HSMP LSP is similar to an MP2MP LSP from RFC 6388, with one difference. When a leaf sends traffic, it goes first and only to the root. The root then places it on the P2MP tree, so it is distributed to all leaves, including the original sender.

To set up the upstream path, LDP ordered mode MUST be used. Ordered mode guarantees that a leaf starts sending to the root only after the upstream path is installed, so packets are not dropped because of an incomplete LSP.

Support is advertised with a new LDP capability. An implementation that supports HSMP LSPs MUST implement the capability procedures for Initialization messages. The HSMP LSP Capability Parameter has type 0x0902, its U-bit MUST be 1, its F-bit MUST be 0, and its Length SHOULD be 1. If a peer has not advertised the capability, label messages using the HSMP FEC elements SHOULD NOT be sent to it.
sections.eli5: Before a stop can send anything back to the hub, the whole road back has to be built first, one piece at a time starting from the hub. That way nothing gets lost on a half-finished road.

sections.title: HSMP FEC Elements and Messages
sections.content:
RFC 7140 defines two new FEC elements: the HSMP-downstream FEC (type 10) and the HSMP-upstream FEC (type 9). Their structure, encoding and error handling are the same as the P2MP FEC element in RFC 6388. If a FEC TLV contains an HSMP FEC element, it MUST be the only element in that TLV.

An HSMP LSP is named by a root node address X and an opaque value Y, written <X, Y>. Each direction has its own Label Mapping, Label Withdraw and Label Release messages, called HSMP-D for downstream and HSMP-U for upstream. The labels in these messages MUST be allocated from the per-platform label space of the sending LSR.
sections.eli5: Each road gets a name tag. One tag says it is the way out from the hub, and the other says it is the way back.

sections.title: Label Mapping at Leaf, Transit and Root Nodes
sections.content:
A node that wants to join the LSP <X, Y> picks as its upstream LSR the LDP peer that is its next hop on the best path to the root X. A node treats any peer that sends it an HSMP-D Label Mapping as a downstream peer.

A leaf sends an HSMP-D Label Mapping to its upstream LSR and then expects an HSMP-U Label Mapping back. When that arrives, it creates state to push the upstream label onto traffic it wants to send over the LSP. Which traffic that is lies outside the scope of the document.

A transit node handles HSMP-D mappings much as in an MP2MP LSP, but it waits for an HSMP-U mapping from its upstream LSR before sending its own HSMP-U mapping downstream. Since upstream packets only ever go to the upstream node, the same upstream label SHOULD be given to all downstream nodes. This differs from MP2MP LSPs, where a distinct label goes to each downstream node.

The root installs the downstream state and an incoming-label state that marks it as the egress Label Edge Router, for example by popping the label stack and passing the packet to an application. The root sends no HSMP-D mapping and receives no HSMP-U mapping.
sections.eli5: Each stop on the way tells the one before it, 'send me stuff this way.' The road back is shared, so every branch uses the same signpost pointing toward the hub.

sections.title: Withdrawal, Upstream Changes and Interfaces
sections.content:
When a leaf no longer needs the LSP, it SHOULD send an HSMP-D Label Withdraw to its upstream LSR and an unsolicited HSMP-U Label Release to say the upstream path is no longer used. A transit node deletes the withdrawn label and, if no downstream state remains, passes the withdrawal upstream. The root does the same but has nothing further upstream to tell.

If a node's upstream LSR changes from U to U', it sets up the LSP toward U' and removes the one toward U. Doing the add before or after the removal is a local matter, and removing first is the recommended default.

The upstream and downstream paths can be co-routed. For a network with symmetric IGP costs, LSR U looks up the best interface and next hop to reach LSR D in its unicast routing table and uses it if LSR D also advertises it over LDP. Where symmetric costs cannot be ensured, static routes on U and D can force a co-routed path. If co-routing is not required, the choice of interface is a local matter.
sections.eli5: When a stop closes, it tells the stop before it to forget the road. If the whole branch is closed, the news travels back toward the hub.

sections.title: LANs, Redundancy and Failure Detection
sections.content:
On a LAN, the downstream path works as for MP2MP LSPs in RFC 6388, using the upstream LSR context label from RFC 5331 and a two-label lookup. The upstream path on a LAN is the same as on other links.

For redundancy, two independent HSMP LSPs can run as active and standby, each with its own root. After the active one fails, the root and leaves switch to the standby. The details of that mechanism are out of scope.

For failure detection, the document reuses LSP ping. The root sends an Echo Request along the downstream path with a Target FEC Stack TLV carrying the HSMP-downstream FEC type and the R flag set to 1. The leaf MUST send the Echo Reply along the HSMP upstream path. New sub-TLVs for this are 29 (HSMP-upstream) and 30 (HSMP-downstream).
sections.eli5: You can build a spare route to a second hub in case the first one breaks. A test message goes out from the hub and the answer comes back along the road home.

sections.title: Security and IANA Assignments
sections.content:
The same security considerations apply as for the MP2MP LSP in RFC 6388 and RFC 6425. The document says the new FEC elements and procedures bring no new security issues beyond those.

IANA allocated two LDP FEC element types (HSMP-upstream 9, HSMP-downstream 10) from the IETF Consensus range, the HSMP LSP Capability TLV 0x0902, and the two LSP ping sub-TLVs 29 and 30.
sections.eli5: The new roads are no riskier than the old ones, so the same safety rules apply. The numbers for the new signs were officially registered.
